critique.finding: It swings as a wide pendulum pulled by gravity {g} with air drag {qd} stealing speed. A faint wobble is left over, but it mostly captures the swing.

headline: Ball swings like a pendulum slowed a little by air.
finding: It swings as a wide pendulum pulled by gravity 9.8227 ± 0.0048 m/s² with air drag 0.0290 ± 0.0045 stealing speed. A faint wobble is left over, but it mostly captures the swing.

eyeball.confidence: low - period estimated by counting ~9.5 swings in 13.4s and L~0.5m; pixel geometry guessed from ~640px frame, damping appears very small
eyeball.law_in_words: pendulum bob projected horizontally is simple harmonic x(t)=xeq + A sin(2pi t/T + phi) with T=2pi sqrt(L/g), L~0.5m, R is pivot-to-bob pixel radius, y follows circular arc y~ybot + R(1-cos(theta)), amplitude A slowly decaying by quadratic air drag

clockCheck.why: Clock checked: gravity came out within 0.16% of Earth’s, so the clip plays in real time.

truth.note: Real footage, filmed by a stranger and shared on Wikimedia Commons: Rhetos of the Mathe-AC Lernwerkstatt Aachen. The true value is standard gravity, 9.807 m/s² (about 9.81). The film’s own description calls it “a pendulum half a metre long”; we told Ansatz only “the string is about fifty centimetres long”. The ± on gravity assumes that stated length is good to 1% (5 mm), a fixed share Ansatz gives every stated length; the fit alone gives ± 0.0048. The agreement says the half metre runs to the bob’s centre, as the film’s description has it: if 50 cm were the string alone, with a bob about 2.3 cm across, the same swing would give g of about 10.0. The film’s own result card, cropped out before the run, gives one swing as about 1.42 s; a 0.5 m pendulum on Earth swings in 1.418 s. The same source’s chalkboard clip defeated SAM 3.1 on 29 October (Proof, where it fails).
